title: Principles live
hookLine: your principles can be rekindled; reviving is in your power (Meditations 7.2)

cards: Camping, second morning, and the fire looks dead. Gray ash, no smoke. But someone who knows fires kneels, brushes the ash aside, and there it is: a dull orange glow underneath.
A little breath, a few dry twigs, and soon there's flame. A practice can look like that ash: the journal you stopped writing, the prayer you used to say, the walk, the reading, the habit of patience.
Book seven of the Meditations begins with a fire.

teach.b: In Meditations seven, two, Marcus asks: how could your principles die? Only if the thoughts that keep them alive go out. The Greek word for principles here is dogmata, the core convictions you live by.
They don't vanish on their own; they fade when you stop thinking them.
And it's in your power, he says, to keep fanning those thoughts into flame. Not a statue that's either standing or broken, but a fire that dims and brightens with what you feed it.
Then the turn: starting to live again is in your power.

teach.h: LOOK AGAIN AS YOU USED TO.
teach.b: Look at things again the way you used to, and that, he says, is the recovery of your life. Notice how small the instruction is. Not reinvent yourself, not wait for a dramatic turning point.
Just look again, the old way, and let the fire catch.

teach.h: A LAPSE IS NOT A VERDICT.
teach.b: It's easy to treat a lapse as a verdict. I stopped meditating, so I'm not someone who meditates. I lost my temper, so patience isn't really me.
Marcus refuses that. Your principles are still there under the ash, as long as you're still willing to think them. A banked fire isn't a dead one.

how: Readers of Marcus often treat a lapse in a practice as something to be relit rather than a failure: they return by doing a small version of it, and by rereading the principles they live by.

o: the rule that only beliefs written down can truly last
Marcus's reminder that convictions fade only if unthought
the rule that a broken habit is gone for good

p: looking at things as you used to

s: Marcus says that once a principle fades, it's gone for good
he says it's in your power to fan the thoughts back into flame.
Meditations 7.2 says beginning to live again is in your power
by looking at things again as you used to.

games.q: you haven't kept a practice you care about for months. what does Marcus say?
o: accept that it isn't really you anymore.
wait for a big turning point.
look at things again as you used to, and relight it now.
games.why: Meditations 7.2: it's in your power to fan your principles into flame and to begin to live again.

practice: Hold in mind one practice or principle that has gone quiet in your life, gratitude, an evening walk, honesty in one hard place, prayer if you pray, without judging how long it's been.
Picture it as a fire under ash, and breathe gently on it by recalling how it felt when it was alive. Then picture doing it once, small.

wordCard.voice: Principles live. Marcus's reminder that convictions fade only when you stop thinking them, and that relighting them is in your power. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: principles, settled convictions; Marcus's word in 7.2.

carryVoice: Your line: rekindle. Looking again, the old way, is how the fire catches. Five hundred eighty-four days, and counting.
